title: Trust People by Giving Them the Toughest Assignments
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The piece argues that handing someone a hard, important assignment is one of the clearest signals of trust a leader can send. Many leaders mistakenly treat the toughest assignments as a punishment, when for a ready team member nothing is more motivating. The authors draw a firm line on readiness: giving a prized assignment to someone unprepared is cruel, but waiting for slam-dunk skills wastes the moment. Good leaders pounce as soon as someone is ready and often make the handoff publicly so the whole team sees trust as the basis of the choice. Delegation is not abdication, though; leaders stack the deck by staying available as a resource and checking in. The counterintuitive conclusion is that the hardest problems are a powerful tool for building trust and projecting confidence in others.
points: Difficult, high-stakes work is presented as a reward and a trust signal, not a punishment, for people who are ready for it.
Readiness is the hinge: assigning a big project to someone unprepared is cruel, while waiting for perfect skills misses the opportunity.
Announcing the handoff publicly tells the wider team that trust is the currency behind the assignment.
Leaders who delegate hard problems should still stack the deck by acting as a resource and checking in.
quotes: Giving people meaty and important assignments is a sign of trust. The best leaders know this and look for opportunities to tell team members they are both ready for an important challenge and they have the utmost confidence and trust in their ability to succeed.

Offering a prized assignment to a colleague who is unprepared for it is cruel. Knowing others will likely fail is no way to inspire confidence. But too many leaders believe giving the hardest assignments to a team member is a punishment.

Knowing the leader trusts them with a key project propels them forward and establishes the confidence needed for great work. The fact that this is a tough and challenging assignment burnishes the trust they feel.

The moment a team member is ready for a big assignment, good leaders pounce. They often announce to colleagues they believe the team member is ready and make the handoff publicly. This tells everyone that trust is the currency that underpins the choice.
In fact, good leaders stack the deck and make sure the assignment will succeed in some measure by serving as a resource and checking in with whatever help the team member needs.
